Pavlivka Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Pavlivka, Ukraine

Demolished. Presumably established in the 18th century alongside the independent Jewish community's emergence, this cemetery was abandoned during WWII and declined until its final demolition by Soviet authorities in the 1970s; the territory is now used for cattle grazing with no visible traces or boundaries. Jews are first mentioned in Poryck (Pavlivka) in 1569, possibly present earlier given a 1554 fire; the community was represented in the Council of the Four Lands, subordinated to Volodymyr-Volynskyi's kehilla in the early 18th century. Population grew from 101 (1784) to 296 (1790), the same period local authorities approved a Jewish printing house (1786), active by 1790. Following Poland's partition, Poryck sat on the Russian-Austrian border, where 19th-century legislation barring Jewish border residence sharply reduced the population - from 1,100 (1847) to just 327 by 1870, before recovering to 1,316 (60%) by 1897. Rabbi Kolonius Kalman Horovitz, grandson of the 'Seer of Lublin,' served the community; WWI brought pogroms and looting. Interwar Hebrew and Yiddish libraries anchored Jewish cultural life; population reached 1,205 by 1921. Refugee resettlement after Nazi occupation on June 23, 1941 swelled the population to 3,000, the same period a ghetto formed; a mass execution of 900 Jews occurred in September 1942.
